title: Functions
summary: Group commands into functions with arguments, answer with a status or a printed value, keep variables local, and share functions through a library.
intro: Once a script grows past a screenful, its pieces need names. A Bash function is a named group of commands that you call like any other command, with arguments of its own. In this lesson you define and call functions, return a status for `if` or a value for `$(...)`, keep their variables private with `local`, and load shared functions from a library file.

steps.title: Define and call
steps.body:
Define a function with a name, `()`, and a body in braces. Call it like a command, with its arguments after the name. Inside the body the arguments are `$1`, `$2`, and so on, and `$#` counts them:

```bash
greet() {
  echo "Hello, $1 (arguments: $#)"
}

greet Ada
greet "Grace Hopper" Linus
```

`"$@"` expands to all the arguments, each one still its own word, so `for a in "$@"` loops over them safely. `$*` joins them into one string, which is handy inside a message. Use `"$@"` unless you want that one string.

Bash runs a script from top to bottom, and a function exists only once Bash has run its definition. So define each function above the first line that calls it. You'll also see `function greet { ...; }` in older scripts. It means the same, but `greet() { ...; }` is the form every shell understands, so prefer it.

examples.title: Greet
examples.prompt: Define two small functions and call them with different arguments.
examples.output:
Hello, Ada!
Hello, Grace Hopper!
Hello, Grace!
Release notes
-------------
examples.explanation: A function's arguments split the same way a command's do. `greet "Grace Hopper"` passes one argument, so `$1` is the full name, while `greet Grace Hopper` passes two, and `greet` only uses the first. In `underline`, `${1//?/-}` replaces every character of `$1` with `-`: `?` matches any one character, and `//` replaces every match, so the line comes out exactly as long as the text.

examples.title: All the arguments
examples.prompt: Show how many arguments a function got, join them into one string, and loop over them with `"$@"`.
examples.code:
show() {
  echo "args: $#, joined: $*"
  for a in "$@"; do
    echo "  [$a]"
  done
}

show "a b" c
show "one two three"
examples.output:
args: 2, joined: a b c
  [a b]
  [c]
args: 1, joined: one two three
  [one two three]
examples.explanation:
`"$@"` keeps every argument exactly as it was passed, so `"a b"` stays one word in the loop. `$*` inside double quotes joins the arguments with spaces into one string, which suits a message. Unquoted, `$*` and `$@` both split again at every space, which is almost never what you want:

```bash
show() {
  for a in $*; do
    echo "[$a]"
  done
}

show "a b" c
```

examples.title: Define before you call
examples.prompt: Call a function on a line above its definition.
examples.explanation:
Bash runs the script one command at a time, and the definition of `greet` hasn't run yet when line 2 calls it. So Bash looks for a program named `greet`, finds none, and fails with status 127, command not found. `exit` without a number ends the script with the status of the command before it, here 127. Move the definition above the first call and the script works:

```bash
greet() {
  echo "Hello, $1!"
}

echo "Greeting the team"
greet Ada || exit
```

practice.title: Banner
practice.prompt:
Write a function that frames a title between two lines of `=`.

1. Write `banner TEXT`. It prints a line of `=` exactly as long as TEXT, then TEXT, then the same line of `=` again.
2. Call `banner` for `Deploy`, `Weekly Report`, and `Q3 Sales Review`, in that order.

Check also calls `banner` with other titles.

Expected output:

```text
======
Deploy
======
=============
Weekly Report
=============
===============
Q3 Sales Review
===============
```
practice.starter:
# TODO: define banner TEXT: a line of = as long as TEXT, then TEXT, then the line again

# TODO: call banner for "Deploy", "Weekly Report" and "Q3 Sales Review"
practice.solution:
banner() {
  line="${1//?/=}"
  echo "$line"
  echo "$1"
  echo "$line"
}

banner "Deploy"
banner "Weekly Report"
banner "Q3 Sales Review"
hints: `banner` works like `underline` from the greet example, with `=` instead of `-` and a second line above the text.
Keep that line in a variable, then `echo` it, `echo "$1"`, and `echo` it again.

steps.title: Return a status or a value
steps.body:
A function gives back two kinds of answer. Its **status** is the status of its last command, or the number after `return`: 0 means success, and 1 to 255 mean failure. That makes a function a condition for `if`, `&&`, and `||`:

```bash
is_even() {
  (( $1 % 2 == 0 ))
}

if is_even 42; then
  echo "42 is even"
fi
is_even 7 || echo "7 is odd"
```

A **value**, like a word or a number, is whatever the function prints. Capture it with `$(...)`, the same as any command's output:

```bash
double() {
  echo "$(( $1 * 2 ))"
}

result=$(double 21)
echo "result: $result"
```

Keep the two apart. `return` takes only a number from 0 to 255, so it can't hand back text. A message for people belongs on stderr, `echo "..." >&2`, so it never ends up inside a captured value. And `exit` inside a function ends the whole script, not just the function.

examples.title: Predicate
examples.prompt: Write a function that answers yes or no with its status, and use it in an `if`.
examples.code:
is_weekend() {
  [[ $1 == Sat || $1 == Sun ]]
}

for day in Fri Sat Sun Mon; do
  if is_weekend "$day"; then
    echo "$day: weekend"
  else
    echo "$day: workday"
  fi
done
examples.output:
Fri: workday
Sat: weekend
Sun: weekend
Mon: workday
examples.explanation: The last command in `is_weekend` is the `[[ ]]` test, so the function's status is the test's: 0 for `Sat` and `Sun`, and 1 for any other day. `if` runs the function and branches on that status, exactly as it does with `grep -q`. A name that reads as a question, like `is_weekend` or `has_errors`, makes the `if` read like a sentence.

examples.title: Value
examples.prompt: Return a string by printing it, and capture it with `$(...)`.
examples.explanation:
`to_upper` prints its answer, and `$(...)` captures what it prints, minus the trailing newline, so the value can go into a variable or the middle of a string. Everything the function prints to stdout lands in the value, so send messages for people to stderr. Here the message shows in the output panel, and the captured name stays clean:

```bash
to_upper() {
  echo "converting $1" >&2
  echo "${1^^}"
}

name=$(to_upper ada)
echo "name: $name"
```

examples.title: Gotchas
examples.prompt: Return a number that's too big for a status, then call a function that runs `exit`.
examples.explanation:
This example breaks two rules on purpose, so ShellCheck is off for it. A status is a single byte, so `return 300` comes back as 300 minus 256, which is 44. And `exit 3` inside `stop` ends the whole script with status 3, so the last `echo` never runs. Use `return` to leave just the function. A `return` with text is an error: Bash prints `numeric argument required`, and the function returns 2:

```bash error
check() {
  return "ok"
}

check
```

practice.title: Validators
practice.prompt:
Check `host port` pairs with two functions that answer with their status.

1. Write `is_port N`, which succeeds when N is a whole number from 1 to 65535.
2. Write `is_hostname S`, which succeeds when S has only letters, digits, dots, and hyphens, and doesn't start with a hyphen.
3. Read `HOST PORT` lines from stdin. For each one, print `HOST:PORT valid`, `HOST:PORT invalid: bad hostname`, or `HOST:PORT invalid: bad port`. Check the hostname first.

Input:

```text
web-1 8080
db.internal 5432
-cache 6379
api 70000
```

Expected output:

```text
web-1:8080 valid
db.internal:5432 valid
-cache:6379 invalid: bad hostname
api:70000 invalid: bad port
```
practice.solution:
port_re='^[0-9]+$'
host_re='^[A-Za-z0-9.][A-Za-z0-9.-]*$'

is_port() {
  [[ $1 =~ $port_re ]] && (( $1 >= 1 && $1 <= 65535 ))
}

is_hostname() {
  [[ $1 =~ $host_re ]]
}

while read -r host port; do
  if ! is_hostname "$host"; then
    echo "$host:$port invalid: bad hostname"
  elif ! is_port "$port"; then
    echo "$host:$port invalid: bad port"
  else
    echo "$host:$port valid"
  fi
done

tests.output:
web-1:8080 valid
db.internal:5432 valid
-cache:6379 invalid: bad hostname
api:70000 invalid: bad port

localhost:22 valid
backup_1:873 invalid: bad hostname
mail.example.com:0 invalid: bad port
proxy:3128x invalid: bad port
queue-1:65535 valid

grafana:3000 valid
WEB-2:65536 invalid: bad port
cache-1: invalid: bad port
10.0.0.5:443 valid

hints: Each function's last command is a test, like in `is_weekend`. `[[ $1 =~ $re ]]` matches a regex kept in a variable.
For a port, match `^[0-9]+$` first, then check `(( $1 >= 1 && $1 <= 65535 ))`, and join the two with `&&`.
In the loop: `if ! is_hostname "$host"; then ... elif ! is_port "$port"; then ... else ... fi`.

steps.title: Local variables and libraries
steps.body:
Variables in Bash are global, even inside a function. A function that sets `i` or `total` changes the caller's `i` or `total`, and that breaks loops in ways that are hard to spot. Declare a function's own variables with `local`, and they exist only while it runs:

```bash
total=100
add_tax() {
  local total=$(( $1 * 120 / 100 ))
  echo "with tax: $total"
}

add_tax 50
echo "total is still $total"
```

Functions that many scripts share go in a library, a file of definitions that you load with `source ./lib/strings.sh`. `source` runs the file in the current shell, so its functions and variables exist afterwards, as if you had typed them in. The `./` makes Bash read the file from this folder instead of searching `PATH` for it.

Longer scripts often put their steps in a `main` function at the top, with helpers below it, and call `main "$@"` on the last line. By then every function is defined, so the order inside the file no longer matters.

examples.title: The clobber bug
examples.prompt: Print three sections, each with a line of dashes made by a helper that forgets `local`.
examples.code:
dashes() {
  line=""
  for ((i = 0; i < $1; i++)); do
    line+="-"
  done
  echo "$line"
}

for ((i = 1; i <= 3; i++)); do
  echo "section $i"
  dashes 9
done
echo "after the loop, i is $i"
examples.output:
section 1
---------
after the loop, i is 10
examples.explanation:
The loop should print three sections, but it prints one. `dashes` uses the same global `i` as the caller and leaves it at 9 when its own loop ends. The caller's `i++` makes that 10, which fails `i <= 3`, so the outer loop stops after one pass. Make `line` and `i` local to `dashes`, and every section prints:

```bash
dashes() {
  local line="" i
  for ((i = 0; i < $1; i++)); do
    line+="-"
  done
  echo "$line"
}

for ((i = 1; i <= 3; i++)); do
  echo "section $i"
  dashes 9
done
echo "after the loop, i is $i"
```

`line+="-"` appends to a string, the same way `lib/strings.sh` builds its lines.

examples.title: A library
examples.prompt: Load `lib/strings.sh`, then use its `trim` and `repeat` functions and its `FILL` variable.
examples.code:
source ./lib/strings.sh

name=$(trim "   Ada Okonkwo   ")
echo "[$name]"
repeat "-" 13
echo "fill: [$FILL]"
examples.explanation: `source` runs `lib/strings.sh` in this script's shell, so the functions `trim` and `repeat` and the variable `FILL` exist from the next line on. `trim` prints its answer, so `$(...)` captures it, while `repeat` prints its line straight to the output. Open `lib/strings.sh` in the Files strip: both functions declare their variables with `local`, so loading the library can't change yours, and it holds only definitions, so sourcing it prints nothing.

examples.title: Structure with main
examples.prompt: Put the script's steps in `main` at the top, with its helpers below it.
examples.output:
== Hosts ==
hosts.txt: 5 lines
== Months ==
a.txt: 12 lines
examples.explanation: `main` calls `header` and `count_lines` above their definitions, and that's fine: nothing runs until `main "$@"` on the last line, and by then all three are defined. Reading top down, you see the steps first and the details after. `main "$@"` hands the script's own arguments to `main`, so the pattern keeps working once a script takes arguments. In `count_lines`, `local n` sits on its own line before `n=$(...)`: written as one line, `local` would hide the exit status of the command inside `$(...)`, and ShellCheck warns about it.

practice.title: Center text
practice.prompt:
Center titles in a line 30 characters wide, padded with the library's fill character.

1. Load `lib/strings.sh` with `source`.
2. Write `center WIDTH TEXT`, which prints TEXT padded on both sides with `"$FILL"` to WIDTH characters. Build each side with `repeat`, and keep the function's variables `local`.
3. When the padding is odd, put the extra character on the right.
4. Center `Status`, `Weekly Report`, and `Incident 1403 Review` in 30 characters.

Check also runs your script with a library whose `FILL` is different, and calls `center` with other widths and titles.

Expected output:

```text
............Status............
........Weekly Report.........
.....Incident 1403 Review.....
```
practice.starter:
# TODO: load lib/strings.sh

# TODO: pad $2 on both sides with "$FILL" to $1 characters, using repeat and local variables
# TODO: when the padding is odd, put the extra character on the right
center() {
  echo "$2"
}

center 30 "Status"
center 30 "Weekly Report"
center 30 "Incident 1403 Review"
practice.solution:
source ./lib/strings.sh

center() {
  local width="$1" text="$2"
  local pad=$(( width - ${#text} ))
  local left=$(( pad / 2 ))
  local right=$(( pad - left ))
  echo "$(repeat "$FILL" "$left")$text$(repeat "$FILL" "$right")"
}

center 30 "Status"
center 30 "Weekly Report"
center 30 "Incident 1403 Review"
hints: Start like the library example, with `source ./lib/strings.sh`. After it, `repeat` and `FILL` exist.
The padding is `width - ${#text}`. The left side gets `pad / 2`, and the right side gets the rest, `pad - left`.
`repeat` ends its line, so capture each side with `$(repeat "$FILL" "$left")`, and print the three pieces with one `echo`.

recap:
- `name() { ...; }` defines a function. Define it above the first line that calls it.
- Inside, `$1`, `$2`, and `$#` work as in a script, and `"$@"` passes on every argument as its own word.
- A function's status is its last command's, or `return N` (0 to 255), so a function can be the condition of `if`, `&&`, and `||`.
- To return a value, print it, and capture it with `$(...)`. Messages for people go to stderr.
- `local` keeps a function's variables private. `exit` in a function ends the whole script.
- `source ./lib/strings.sh` loads a library, and `main "$@"` on the last line runs a script whose `main` sits at the top.
